282:
Augustine considered it 'not incredible' that some of the faithful are saved through a purifying fire after death to a greater or lesser extent (*Enchiridion* 69; *City of God* 21.26), while distinguishing temporary punishments (21.13) from eternal ones. Gregory the Great (*Dialogues* book 4, c. 594) taught that for certain lighter faults there is a purging fire before judgment, citing Matt 12:32 and 1 Cor 3, and told stories of souls freed by Masses; this greatly shaped medieval piety. Jacques Le Goff dated the 'birth' of purgatory as a distinct place to the late twelfth century, when the noun purgatorium appeared; critics say he overstated the novelty, since the concept was much older than the noun.

Lyon II (1274) included in the Byzantine emperor's profession that souls who die in charity before making satisfaction are purified after death by purgatorial or cleansing penalties, helped by the suffrages of the living. Florence (1439), in the decree of union with the Greeks, restated this; at the council the Greek spokesman Mark of Ephesus objected to the idea of a purifying material fire and of satisfaction, accepting an intermediate state and prayer for the dead. Trent (1563) affirmed purgatory and the help of suffrages, especially the Mass, while instructing bishops to avoid curious questions and superstitions. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1030-1032) presents it as final purification rather than primarily a place of fire.

The Reformers rejected purgatory as lacking scriptural support and undermining Christ's finished work and justification by faith; abuse of indulgences triggered Luther's 95 Theses (1517). Some modern Protestants (e.g. C. S. Lewis, Jerry Walls) have argued for a purgatory of sanctification rather than satisfaction.
283: The Christian synthesis of soul and resurrection
284: From the third century, Christian theologians increasingly combined the biblical resurrection hope with a philosophical doctrine of an immaterial, naturally immortal soul. The two were held together: the soul survives death and is judged, and will be reunited with the body at the last day. This synthesis became standard in East and West, but its balance and biblical basis have been questioned in modern scholarship.
287:
Earlier writers such as Justin, Theophilus and Irenaeus stressed that only God is immortal by nature (1 Tim 6:16). By contrast, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine engaged Platonist philosophy and argued for the soul's natural immortality, while insisting on the resurrection. Aquinas, using Aristotle, made the soul the 'form' of the body: it subsists after death but is incomplete without the body, which gives resurrection a philosophical necessity. The Fifth Lateran Council (1513) condemned the view that the intellectual soul is mortal.

In 1956 Oscar Cullmann's lecture *Immortality of the Soul or Resurrection of the Dead?* contrasted Socrates' calm death with Jesus' anguish, arguing that the New Testament knows resurrection, not natural immortality; this was widely influential and much criticized. Defenders such as John W. Cooper argue that the Bible itself supports a 'holistic dualism' with a conscious intermediate state, and that the classical synthesis did not abandon resurrection.
289: In the sixteenth century, some reformers and radical groups revived the view that souls sleep or die until the resurrection (Christian mortalism), partly in reaction to purgatory and the cult of the saints. Calvin's first theological work attacked it, and the Reformed and Lutheran confessions affirmed a conscious intermediate state, though Luther himself often used the language of sleep.
295:
Luther frequently described death as a deep sleep from which the believer will awake at the resurrection, but scholars debate whether he held to unconscious soul sleep or a restful, conscious state with God; his statements vary. Tyndale, against Thomas More, argued that teaching souls already in heaven undermined the resurrection hope Paul used to comfort the Thessalonians. Calvin wrote *Psychopannychia* (drafted c. 1534, published 1542) against Anabaptists who taught soul sleep, arguing from Luke 23:43, Phil 1:23 and Rev 6:9 for conscious rest with Christ.

The Westminster Confession (32.1) states that the souls of the righteous are received into the highest heavens and those of the wicked cast into hell, awaiting the resurrection, and that Scripture acknowledges no other place. Mortalism continued in English thought (Milton, Hobbes), and later in Seventh-day Adventism, Christadelphians and Jehovah's Witnesses. Some modern biblical scholars find the mortalist reading closer to Hebrew anthropology, while most systematic theologians retain a conscious intermediate state.
296: The beatific vision and Benedictus Deus (1336)
297: In Western theology the final joy of the saints came to be described as the 'beatific vision': seeing God's essence directly with the intellect, elevated by grace. After a controversy provoked by Pope John XXII, Pope Benedict XII defined in *Benedictus Deus* (1336) that fully purified souls see the divine essence immediately after death, before the resurrection. Eastern Orthodoxy speaks instead of seeing the uncreated light and participating in God's energies, not his essence.
301:
Augustine closes *City of God* (22.29) speculating how the saints will see God, perhaps even with their resurrected bodily eyes perceiving God in all things. Aquinas argued that final human happiness consists in the vision of the divine essence, which exceeds natural capacity and requires the 'light of glory'.

In sermons of 1331-1332 Pope John XXII suggested that the souls of the saints do not see God's essence until the general resurrection, seeing only the humanity of Christ in the meantime. This provoked strong opposition from theologians at Paris; he qualified his view shortly before his death in 1334. His successor Benedict XII defined in *Benedictus Deus* (1336) that the souls of the saints, once purified, see the divine essence face to face immediately after death, and that those dying in mortal sin descend at once to hell; this effectively defined the immediacy of the individual judgment in Latin theology.

In the same decade Gregory Palamas defended Eastern monks who claimed to see the uncreated light of Tabor, distinguishing God's unknowable essence from his energies, in which creatures participate. Orthodox theologians have therefore criticized the Western idea of seeing the divine essence, while Catholic theologians argue the positions can be reconciled. Protestants have generally affirmed the vision of God with less philosophical precision; there has been renewed interest in the doctrine (e.g. Hans Boersma, *Seeing God*, 2018).
303: In the Greek patristic and Orthodox tradition, the goal of salvation is theosis or deification: becoming by grace what God is by nature, sharing in the divine life without ceasing to be creatures. The final state is not static rest but endless growth into God, beginning now in the sacraments and ascetic life, continuing after death and fulfilled in the resurrection and transfigured cosmos.
307:
Irenaeus speaks of the Word becoming what we are so that we might become what he is (preface to book 5); Athanasius gives the classic form, that God became human so that humans might be made divine (*On the Incarnation* 54.3). Gregory of Nyssa described the life of the saints, in this age and the next, as endless progress (epektasis) into the infinite God, so that perfection itself is ever-growing. Maximus the Confessor developed a cosmic vision in which humanity, united to God in Christ, mediates the transfiguration of all creation. Palamas framed deification as participation in God's uncreated energies.

In Orthodox eschatology the same divine glory is experienced differently according to the state of the person: as light and joy by those who love God, and as burning by those who reject him (an idea traced to Isaac the Syrian and developed by modern writers). This reframes heaven and hell as relational rather than primarily spatial; critics argue it can blur the biblical language of judgment and separation.

Shift: deification language faded from much Western theology after the medieval period (though present in Aquinas and some mystics) and was revived in the twentieth century through Orthodox theologians in the West, Catholic ressourcement, and Protestant studies of 'union with Christ' (e.g. the Finnish Luther research led by Tuomo Mannermaa).
308: From resurrection hope to 'going to heaven'
309: Many historians and theologians argue that over the centuries popular Christian hope shifted from the resurrection of the body in a renewed creation to the soul's departure to heaven at death. N. T. Wright and others call for recovering the earlier emphasis; critics reply that the tradition always confessed resurrection and that the immediate heavenly hope is also biblical, so the contrast is overdrawn.
317:
The argument: early creeds and Fathers focused on resurrection and renewal; Platonist thought, monastic spirituality, the decline of chiliasm, the doctrine of immediate judgment and the beatific vision (1336), and later Pietist and revivalist preaching made 'going to heaven when you die' the centre of popular hope. McDannell and Lang trace changing images of heaven, from a theocentric vision of God to the nineteenth-century homely heaven of reunited families. Pelikan's study of the early Fathers (1961) explored how they combined Greek ideas of immortality with biblical resurrection. Cullmann (1956) sharply contrasted immortality with resurrection. Wright argues that the New Testament's 'heaven' is the temporary resting place, and the final hope is 'life after life after death' in a new creation, with large implications for ethics and mission.

Critiques and responses: Bynum shows that medieval Western theology cared intensely about the resurrected body, so the 'loss of resurrection' narrative oversimplifies. Cooper and others argue that a conscious heavenly intermediate state is itself New Testament teaching (2 Cor 5:8, Phil 1:23), so popular piety is incomplete rather than mistaken. Some Catholic and Orthodox writers add that union with God, not the material setting, is the heart of the final state, and that new-creation rhetoric can become this-worldly. Wright's defenders reply that he affirms the intermediate state and the vision of God, and objects only to the displacement of resurrection.
